passage:
In February, Javier had filled Hiroshi's tiny Lisbon flat with yellow tulips and left notes on the bathroom mirror: You are the best thing that ever happened to me. By June the notes were gone.
Now Hiroshi stood at the stove at eleven at night, stirring the bean stew Javier used to love, because yesterday Javier had called the flat "depressing" and Hiroshi "boring lately". He had already changed his shirt twice.
The key turned. Javier walked past the table, glanced at the pot and said, "I ate."
Hiroshi ate alone, scrolling back through old messages from February. Good morning, beautiful. Can't wait to see you. He read them the way people reread a favourite book, hoping the ending might change. Then he opened a message to his sister in Kyoto, typed "Is it normal to feel like I'm auditioning in my own home?", and for the first time, pressed send.

qa.q: What did Javier fill the flat with in February?
qa.a: Javier filled the flat with yellow tulips.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi hope for when he reread the February messages?
qa.a: He was hoping the warm Javier of February would come back, the way someone rereads a favourite book wishing the ending might change.

qa.q: Why was pressing send to his sister a turning point for Hiroshi?
qa.a: Naming the feeling to someone outside let him check what was happening; the gap between February's tulips and June's "I ate" is the pattern, and support can help him stop auditioning for warmth.

qa.q: What would change if Hiroshi judged things by June instead of by February?
qa.a: He would see the criticism and absence as how things are now, not a phase he can fix by cooking or changing shirts, and could decide from there.

grounding: A man in his twenties, once flooded with tulips and notes from Javier, now meets criticism and absence and works to win back the early warmth before naming the gap.

passage:
The shuttlecock hit the net and Chinmay didn't even chase it. Across the community centre hall, Bhupen was laughing with the doubles group and hadn't looked at him once all evening.
Four months ago it had been different. Bhupen had waited after every session with two cups of cutting chai, called him "the only person who really gets me", and sent poems at midnight. Now the messages were short: "Busy." "You're too clingy." "Your serve is embarrassing."
So Chinmay had started coming early to practise serves alone, rereading his texts before sending them, apologising for things he couldn't name.
In the changing room, the coach, Mrs Fernandes, paused by the bench. "You used to smile on this court," she said. "Everything okay?"
Chinmay almost said fine. Instead he said, "I keep trying to get back to how it was at the start." She sat down beside him and listened.

qa.q: What did Bhupen bring after every session four months ago?
qa.a: Bhupen waited after every session with two cups of cutting chai.

qa.q: Why had Chinmay started apologising for things he couldn't name?
qa.a: He felt anxious and at fault, hoping that if he tried hard enough he could win back Bhupen's early warmth.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make in the changing room, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He chose not to say fine and told Mrs Fernandes the truth, which let someone outside listen and helped him see the pattern instead of just trying harder.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes see the change in Chinmay?
qa.a: She notices he no longer smiles on the court and guesses something is weighing on him, so she makes time to listen rather than only coaching his serve.

grounding: A young man whose early flood of chai and midnight poems from Bhupen has shrunk into curt criticism works hard to earn back the warmth, then names the gap to his coach.

passage:
You want to know why I'm so tired all the time? Okay. You're my oldest friend, so I'll say it. I'm Deepika, and I keep trying to get back the first three months with Harish.
In the beginning, it was flowers at my office, a surprise trip to Goa, messages every hour: "You're perfect. I've never been this happy." I'd never felt so loved.
And then, around month four, it just… shrank. He stopped asking about my day. Then he started correcting things. My clothes. How I laugh. How I talk to my mother on the phone. Some days he doesn't reply at all.
So I try harder. I cook what he likes. I wear what he likes. And sometimes, for a day, he's sweet again, and I think, there he is.
When I say it out loud to you… the gap is huge, isn't it? Those two people don't feel like the same man.

qa.q: What surprise trip did Harish plan early on?
qa.a: A surprise trip to Goa.

qa.q: What is Deepika feeling as she describes trying harder?
qa.a: Deepika feels exhausted and confused, hoping to win back the early warmth while starting to see the gap between the two phases.

qa.q: What could Deepika do next, with her friend's help?
qa.a: She could keep talking to her friend, write down the pattern, and speak to a counsellor about what she is experiencing.

qa.q: What does the friend likely notice while listening?
qa.a: The friend probably notices how tired and changed Deepika is, and feels worried about the big gap she describes.

grounding: A young adult describes a flood of early affection shrinking into criticism and silence, and working hard to earn back the warmth.

passage:
March. Mahima, Sonali's new colleague, adored her. Coffee every morning. Lunch every day. "You're the only one here who gets me." Gifts on Sonali's desk. Sonali felt lucky.
May. Mahima started missing coffee without saying why. At lunch, she laughed at Sonali's ideas in front of others. When Sonali asked if something was wrong, Mahima said, "You're so needy lately." Sonali lay awake that night, going over what she'd done.
July. Sonali was bringing Mahima's favourite snacks, staying late to help with her reports, laughing at every joke. Sometimes Mahima was warm again for an afternoon, and Sonali felt a rush of relief. Then cold again.
One Sunday, her sister listened to all of it and said quietly, "Sonali, you're describing two different people. March-Mahima and July-Mahima. You keep chasing March."
Sonali stared at her tea. Her sister was right. The gap was the pattern.

qa.q: What did Mahima call Sonali in May?
qa.a: She said, "You're so needy lately."

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when Mahima was warm again for an afternoon?
qa.a: Sonali felt a rush of relief, which kept her working hard to win back the early warmth.

qa.q: What helped Sonali see the pattern?
qa.a: Talking to her sister, someone outside the situation, who named the gap between March and July.

qa.q: How does Sonali's sister see the situation?
qa.a: Her sister sees two different phases of the same person and worries that Sonali is chasing the early warmth.

grounding: It shows a young adult flooded with early attention by a colleague, then met with criticism and coldness, and working to earn back the warmth.

passage:
Gurleen, you asked why I was so careful when you told me about your new boyfriend. Let your Jasleen Bua tell you.
When I was twenty-four, a man courted me like a film hero. He came to my college every day with a rose. Within a month, he wanted to marry.
After the engagement, the roses stopped. He criticised my friends. My laugh was too loud. My job was a waste of time. When I cried, he said I was too sensitive. And once in a while, he'd be the rose man again, and I'd feel I'd done something right.
I spent a year trying to earn back that first month.
Your Dadi finally sat me down and said, "Beta, the man with the roses and the man who shouts are the same man." I broke the engagement that winter.
I'm not saying your boy is like that. I'm saying watch the gap.

qa.q: What did the man bring to Jasleen's college every day?
qa.a: A rose.

qa.q: How did young Jasleen feel when he became the rose man again?
qa.a: She felt relieved and hopeful, as if she had done something right, which kept her trying to earn back the first month.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Jasleen?
qa.a: Gurleen's Dadi told her the man with the roses and the man who shouts are the same man, and Jasleen broke the engagement that winter.

qa.q: How might Gurleen's Dadi have felt watching Jasleen that year?
qa.a: The Dadi was probably worried and protective, seeing Jasleen chase the early warmth while being criticised.

grounding: An aunt recalls a courtship flood that turned into criticism, her efforts to earn back the early warmth, and learning to watch the gap.

passage: The power went out in the flat at eight, just as Vandana was plating the rajma Amandeep had once called "the best thing I've ever eaten". That was in March, when he sent flowers to her office every Friday and said he'd never met anyone so bright. Now it was November. By candlelight she went over her day: she had ironed his shirts, left her book club early, and not mentioned her promotion, because last time he'd called it showing off. He came in, glanced at the plate, and said the rajma was cold. "The power..." she began. He was already on his phone. Vandana sat in the dark kitchen, scrolling back to their March messages, the hearts, the "my queen". If she just tried harder, surely that man would come back. Then she noticed she had stopped telling her sister anything, and she dialled her number.

qa.q: What had Amandeep once called the rajma?
qa.a: He had once called it the best thing he'd ever eaten.

qa.q: Why was Vandana trying so hard as she went over her day?
qa.a: Vandana felt anxious and desperate to earn back the March warmth, hoping that if she tried harder the old Amandeep would return.

qa.q: What step does Vandana take at the end, and why might it help?
qa.a: She dials her sister after noticing she had stopped telling her anything; reconnecting with someone outside the relationship can help her see the pattern clearly.

qa.q: How might Vandana's sister see the change from March to November?
qa.a: Her sister may have noticed Vandana growing quieter and busier pleasing Amandeep, and may feel both relieved and concerned when the call finally comes.

grounding: Shows a flood of early attention shrinking into criticism and absence, with the receiver working hard to win back the early warmth.
